families.s: HSE waste machinery guarding, cleaning and stored-energy isolation guidance
families.t: balers, compactors, conveyors, shredders, trommels, fixed guards, interlocks, electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic isolation, stored energy and competence
f: Waste plants use balers, compactors, conveyors, shredders, trommels and other high-risk machinery.
Risk assessments and maintained safe systems are required for every machine and intervention task.
Fixed guards should be secured so moving parts cannot be reached during operation.
Removed guards must be replaced before machinery returns to service.
Cleaning, repair and maintenance require secure isolation from power sources.
Isolation should include electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic energy where applicable.
Stored energy must be dissipated or restrained before entry into danger zones.
Work should be planned, organised and carried out by people competent for the machine and task.
families.g: Waste-machinery risk depends on equipment and movement, feed and access points, guarding and interlocks, intervention frequency, energy sources and storage, isolation, maintenance and competence.

families.s: HSE baler, compactor and recovered-paper safe-operation guidance
families.t: feed openings, loading, blockages, compacting pressure, guarding, isolation, skips, tipping, sheeting, maintenance and supervision
f: Recovered-paper guidance covers balers, compactors, skips, tipping, sheeting and vehicle maintenance.
Baler and compactor feed areas should prevent access to dangerous moving parts.
Loading methods should keep people clear of rams, chambers and moving waste.
Blockage clearing should use a defined safe system rather than reaching into operating equipment.
Electrical, hydraulic and stored mechanical energy should be isolated before entry or maintenance.
Guards, interlocks and emergency controls require routine inspection and maintenance.
Associated skips and lifting systems should be checked for attachment and hydraulic defects.
Operators need equipment-specific instruction, training, supervision and defect-reporting arrangements.
families.g: Baler and compactor risk depends on machine design and pressure, feed and blockage access, guarding and controls, waste characteristics, isolation, associated containers and lifting, maintenance and competence.

families.s: HSE materials-recovery-facility conveyor ergonomics and noise-control guidance
families.t: picking stations, conveyor height, throughput, material depth, reaching, twisting, repetitive work, noise action levels and engineering controls
f: Conveyors can reduce bulk lifting but poorly designed picking stations can create repetitive upper-limb and back risk.
Picking stations should minimise leaning, stooping, twisting and over-reaching.
Assessment should consider conveyor height and size.
Material type, throughput and depth affect the physical demands on sorters.
Handling method and workstation layout should match worker reach and posture.
Many materials-recovery facilities generate noise above regulatory action levels.
Noise assessment should identify the equipment and tasks creating exposure.
Engineering, enclosure, maintenance, job design and hearing protection should be combined according to the risk.
families.g: MRF ergonomic and noise risk depends on conveyor and station design, material and throughput, reach and repetition, staffing and rotation, equipment noise, enclosure, maintenance and exposure time.

families.s: HSE materials-recovery-facility dust, microorganisms and occupational-hygiene guidance
families.t: organic dust, fungi, bacteria, endotoxins, COSHH assessment, ventilation, LEV, RPE, hygiene, surveillance and training
f: Waste sorting can generate organic dust containing airborne microorganisms and toxic by-products.
Workers may be exposed to fungi, bacteria and endotoxins.
General airborne dust can exceed levels at which it is treated as hazardous to health.
A suitable COSHH assessment should identify dusty operations and exposed groups.
Ventilation and local exhaust should control inhalation exposure where practicable.
Suitable RPE may be needed for residual or high-exposure tasks.
Adequate welfare, hygiene, training and supervision are required.
Risk-based health surveillance can help identify respiratory effects and failures in exposure control.
families.g: MRF bioaerosol risk depends on waste composition and age, process and disturbance, dust generation, enclosure and ventilation, proximity and duration, hygiene, RPE, maintenance and susceptibility.

families.s: HSE WEEE hazardous-component and substance-exposure guidance
families.t: arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury, flame retardants, fluorescent tubes, cathode-ray tubes, component removal, containment and exposure control
f: Waste electrical and electronic equipment contains a complex mix of product types and hazardous materials.
Potential substances include arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and some flame retardants.
Breaking fluorescent tubes can release mercury.
Cathode-ray-tube processing can release lead and other hazardous substances.
Some hazardous components should be removed before shredding or other treatment.
Disassembly and treatment methods should prevent uncontrolled breakage and release.
Containment, extraction, cleaning and PPE should reflect the specific component and substance.
Exposure assessment and monitoring should verify that lead, mercury and other hazards are adequately controlled.
families.g: WEEE substance risk depends on equipment type and age, hazardous components, dismantling and breakage method, containment and extraction, cleaning, waste storage, monitoring and competence.
